like an elephant at the head of the battle.

15.1.s:
Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṁ,
… pe
…
nibbisaṁ bhatako yathā.

Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā,
… pe
…
bhavanetti samūhatā.
15.1.e:
I’ve served the Teacher
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
The heavy burden is laid down,
the leash to existence is eradicated.

15.1.s:
Yassa catthāya pabbajito,
agārasmānagāriyaṁ;
So me attho anuppatto,
kiṁ me saddhivihārinā”ti.
15.1.e:
I’ve attained the goal
for the sake of which I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness—
what use do I have for protégés?”

15.2.s:
“Manussabhūtaṁ sambuddhaṁ,
Attadantaṁ samāhitaṁ;
Iriyamānaṁ brahmapathe,
Cittassūpasame rataṁ.
15.2.e:
Awakened as a human being,
self-tamed and immersed in samādhi,
following the spiritual path,
he loves peace of mind.

15.2.s:
Yaṁ manussā namassanti,
sabbadhammāna pāraguṁ;
Devāpi taṁ namassanti,
iti me arahato sutaṁ.
15.2.e:
Revered by people,
gone beyond all things,
even the gods revere him;
so I’ve heard from the perfected one.

15.2.s:
Sabbasaṁyojanātītaṁ,
vanā nibbanamāgataṁ;
Kāmehi nekkhammarataṁ,
muttaṁ selāva kañcanaṁ.
15.2.e:
He has transcended all fetters,
and escaped from entanglements.
Delighting to renounce sensual pleasures,
he’s freed like lustrous gold from stone.

15.2.s:
Sa ve accaruci nāgo,
himavāvaññe siluccaye;
Sabbesaṁ nāganāmānaṁ,
saccanāmo anuttaro.
15.2.e:
That giant outshines all,
like the Himalaya beside other mountains.
Of all those named “giant”,
he is truly named, supreme.

15.2.s:
Nāgaṁ vo kittayissāmi,
na hi āguṁ karoti so;
Soraccaṁ avihiṁsā ca,
pādā nāgassa te duve.
15.2.e:
I shall extol the giant for you,
for he does nothing monstrous.
gentleness and harmlessness
are two feet of the giant.

15.2.s:
Sati ca sampajaññañca,
caraṇā nāgassa tepare;
Saddhāhattho mahānāgo,
upekkhāsetadantavā.
15.2.e:
Mindfulness and awareness
are his two other feet.
Faith is the giant’s trunk,
and equanimity his white tusks.

15.2.s:
Sati gīvā siro paññā,
vīmaṁsā dhammacintanā;
Dhammakucchisamāvāso,
viveko tassa vāladhi.
15.2.e:
Mindfulness is his neck, his head is wisdom—
investigation and thinking about principles.
His belly is the sacred hearth of the Dhamma,
and his tail is seclusion.

15.2.s:
So jhāyī assāsarato,
ajjhattaṁ susamāhito;
Gacchaṁ samāhito nāgo,
ṭhito nāgo samāhito.
15.2.e:
Practicing absorption, enjoying the breath,
he is serene within.
The giant is serene when walking,
the giant is serene when standing,

15.2.s:
Sayaṁ samāhito nāgo,
nisinnopi samāhito;
Sabbattha saṁvuto nāgo,
esā nāgassa sampadā.
15.2.e:
the giant is serene when lying down,
and when sitting, the giant is serene.
The giant is restrained everywhere:
this is the accomplishment of the giant.

15.2.s:
Bhuñjati anavajjāni,
sāvajjāni na bhuñjati;
Ghāsamacchādanaṁ laddhā,
sannidhiṁ parivajjayaṁ.
15.2.e:
He eats blameless things,
he doesn’t eat blameworthy things.
When he gets food and clothes,
he avoids storing them up.

15.2.s:
Saṁyojanaṁ aṇuṁ thūlaṁ,
sabbaṁ chetvāna bandhanaṁ;
Yena yeneva gacchati,
anapekkhova gacchati.
15.2.e:
Having severed all bonds,
fetters large and small,
wherever he goes,
he goes without concern.

15.2.s:
Yathāpi udake jātaṁ,
puṇḍarīkaṁ pavaḍḍhati;
Nopalippati toyena,
sucigandhaṁ manoramaṁ.
15.2.e:
A white lotus,
fragrant and delightful,
sprouts in water and grows there,
but the water doesn’t cling to it.

15.2.s:
Tatheva ca loke jāto,
buddho loke viharati;
Nopalippati lokena,
toyena padumaṁ yathā.
15.2.e:
Just so the Buddha is born in the world,
and lives in the world,
but the world doesn’t stick to him,
as water does not stick to the lotus.

15.2.s:
Mahāgini pajjalito,
anāhāropasammati;
Aṅgāresu ca santesu,
nibbutoti pavuccati.
15.2.e:
A great blazing fire
dies down when the fuel runs out.
And when the coals have gone out
it’s said to be “quenched”.

15.2.s:
Atthassāyaṁ viññāpanī,
upamā viññūhi desitā;
Viññissanti mahānāgā,
nāgaṁ nāgena desitaṁ.
15.2.e:
This simile is taught by the discerning
to express the meaning clearly.
Great giants will understand
what the giant taught the giant.

15.2.s:
Vītarāgo vītadoso,
Vītamoho anāsavo;
Sarīraṁ vijahaṁ nāgo,
Parinibbissatyanāsavo”ti.
15.2.e:
Free of greed, free of hate,
free of delusion, undefiled;
the giant, giving up his body,
undefiled, will be fully quenched.

16.1.s:
“Yaññatthaṁ vā dhanatthaṁ vā,
ye hanāma mayaṁ pure;
Avasesaṁ bhayaṁ hoti,
vedhanti vilapanti ca.
16.1.e:
“Those who we killed in the past,
whether for sacrifice or for wealth,
without exception were afraid;
they trembled and they squealed.

16.1.s:
Tassa te natthi bhītattaṁ,
bhiyyo vaṇṇo pasīdati;
Kasmā na paridevesi,
evarūpe mahabbhaye”.
16.1.e:
But you’re not scared;
you look even calmer than before.
Why don’t you cry out
in such a terrifying situation?”

16.1.s:
“Natthi cetasikaṁ dukkhaṁ,
anapekkhassa gāmaṇi;
Atikkantā bhayā sabbe,
khīṇasaṁyojanassa ve.
16.1.e:
“There isn’t any mental suffering
for one without concern, village chief.
All fears are left behind
by one whose fetters have ended.

16.1.s:
Khīṇāya bhavanettiyā,
diṭṭhe dhamme yathātathe;
Na bhayaṁ maraṇe hoti,
bhāranikkhepane yathā.
16.1.e:
When the leash to existence is ended,
and the truth is seen as it is,
there is no fear of death;
it’s like laying down a burden.

16.1.s:
Suciṇṇaṁ brahmacariyaṁ me,
maggo cāpi subhāvito;
Maraṇe me bhayaṁ natthi,
rogānamiva saṅkhaye.
16.1.e:
I’ve lived the spiritual life well,
and developed the path well, too.
I do not fear death;
it’s like the passing of a disease.

16.1.s:
Suciṇṇaṁ brahmacariyaṁ me,
maggo cāpi subhāvito;
Nirassādā bhavā diṭṭhā,
visaṁ pitvāva chaḍḍitaṁ.
16.1.e:
I’ve lived the spiritual life well,
and developed the path well, too.
I’ve seen that there’s nothing gratifying in existences,
like someone who has tasted poison, <j>then thrown it out.

16.1.s:
Pāragū anupādāno,
katakicco anāsavo;
Tuṭṭho āyukkhayā hoti,
mutto āghātanā yathā.
16.1.e:
One who has gone beyond, without grasping,
they’ve completed the task <j>and are free of defilements.
They are content at the end of life,
like someone released from execution.

16.1.s:
Uttamaṁ dhammataṁ patto,
sabbaloke anatthiko;
Ādittāva gharā mutto,
maraṇasmiṁ na socati.
16.1.e:
Having realized the supreme Dhamma,
without needing anything in the whole world,
one doesn’t grieve at death;
for it’s like escaping from a burning house.

16.1.s:
Yadatthi saṅgataṁ kiñci,
bhavo vā yattha labbhati;
Sabbaṁ anissaraṁ etaṁ,
iti vuttaṁ mahesinā.
16.1.e:
Whatever has come to pass,
wherever life is obtained,
there is no Lord of all that:
so said the great seer.

16.1.s:
Yo taṁ tathā pajānāti,
yathā buddhena desitaṁ;
Na gaṇhāti bhavaṁ kiñci,
sutattaṁva ayoguḷaṁ.
16.1.e:
Whoever understands this
as it was taught by the Buddha
doesn’t grab on to any new life,
like you wouldn’t grab a hot iron ball.

16.1.s:
Na me hoti ‘ahosin’ti,
‘bhavissan’ti na hoti me;
Saṅkhārā vigamissanti,
tattha kā paridevanā.
16.1.e:
It doesn’t occur to me, ‘I existed in the past’;
nor, ‘I will exist in the future’.
Conditions will vanish—
why weep over that?

16.1.s:
Suddhaṁ dhammasamuppādaṁ,
Suddhaṁ saṅkhārasantatiṁ;
Passantassa yathābhūtaṁ,
Na bhayaṁ hoti gāmaṇi.
16.1.e:
Seeing truly
the bare arising of phenomena,
and the bare process of conditions,
there is no fear, village chief.

16.1.s:
Tiṇakaṭṭhasamaṁ lokaṁ,
yadā paññāya passati;
Mamattaṁ so asaṁvindaṁ,
‘natthi me’ti na socati.
16.1.e:
The world is like grass and sticks:
when this is seen with wisdom,
not finding any possessiveness,
you won’t grieve, thinking ‘I don’t have it’.

16.1.s:
Ukkaṇṭhāmi sarīrena,
bhavenamhi anatthiko;
Soyaṁ bhijjissati kāyo,
añño ca na bhavissati.
16.1.e:
I’m fed up with the body;
I have no need for another life.
This body will be broken up,
and there won’t be another.

16.1.s:
Yaṁ vo kiccaṁ sarīrena,
taṁ karotha yadicchatha;
Na me tappaccayā tattha,
doso pemañca hehiti”.
16.1.e:
Do what you want
with my corpse.
I won’t be angry or attached
on account of that.”

16.1.s:
Tassa taṁ vacanaṁ sutvā,
abbhutaṁ lomahaṁsanaṁ;
Satthāni nikkhipitvāna,
māṇavā etadabravuṁ.
16.1.e:
When they heard these words,
so astonishing and hair-raising,
the young men laid down their swords
and spoke these words:

16.1.s:
“Kiṁ bhadante karitvāna,
ko vā ācariyo tava;
Kassa sāsanamāgamma,
labbhate taṁ asokatā”.
16.1.e:
“What have you practiced, Venerable?
And who is your tutor?
Whose instructions do we follow
to gain the sorrowless state?”

16.1.s:
“Sabbaññū sabbadassāvī,
jino ācariyo mama;
Mahākāruṇiko satthā,
sabbalokatikicchako.
16.1.e:
“The knower of all, the seer of all:
the victor is my tutor.
He is a Teacher of great compassion,
healer of the whole world.

16.1.s:
Tenāyaṁ desito dhammo,
khayagāmī anuttaro;
Tassa sāsanamāgamma,
labbhate taṁ asokatā”.
16.1.e:
He taught this Dhamma,
leading to ending, unsurpassed.
Following his instructions,
you can gain the sorrowless state.”

16.1.s:
Sutvāna corā isino subhāsitaṁ,
Nikkhippa satthāni ca āvudhāni ca;
Tamhā ca kammā viramiṁsu eke,
Eke ca pabbajjamarocayiṁsu.
16.1.e:
When the bandits heard the good words of the seer,
they laid down their swords and weapons.
Some refrained from their former deeds,
while others chose the going-forth.

16.1.s:
Te pabbajitvā sugatassa sāsane,
Bhāvetva bojjhaṅgabalāni paṇḍitā;
Udaggacittā sumanā katindriyā,
Phusiṁsu nibbānapadaṁ asaṅkhatanti.
16.1.e:
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Holy One,
those astute ones developed <j>the awakening factors and the powers.
Elated, happy, their faculties complete,
they realized the state of extinguishment, <j>the unconditioned.

16.2.s:
“Samaṇassa ahu cintā,
pārāpariyassa bhikkhuno;
Ekakassa nisinnassa,
pavivittassa jhāyino.
16.2.e:
This thought came to the ascetic,
the monk Pārāsariya,
as he was seated alone
meditating in seclusion:

16.2.s:
Kimānupubbaṁ puriso,
kiṁ vataṁ kiṁ samācāraṁ;
Attano kiccakārīssa,
na ca kañci viheṭhaye.
16.2.e:
“Following what procedure,
what observance, what conduct,
may a person do what they need for themselves,
without harming anyone else?

16.2.s:
Indriyāni manussānaṁ,
hitāya ahitāya ca;
Arakkhitāni ahitāya,
rakkhitāni hitāya ca.
16.2.e:
The faculties of human beings
can lead to both welfare and harm.
Unguarded they lead to harm;
guarded they lead to welfare.

16.2.s:
Indriyāneva sārakkhaṁ,
indriyāni ca gopayaṁ;
Attano kiccakārīssa,
na ca kañci viheṭhaye.
16.2.e:
By protecting the faculties,
taking care of the faculties,
I can do what I need for myself
without harming anyone else.

16.2.s:
Cakkhundriyañce rūpesu,
gacchantaṁ anivārayaṁ;
Anādīnavadassāvī,
so dukkhā na hi muccati.
16.2.e:
If your eye wanders
among sights without check,
not seeing the danger,
you’re not freed from suffering.

16.2.s:
Sotindriyañce saddesu,
gacchantaṁ anivārayaṁ;
Anādīnavadassāvī,
so dukkhā na hi muccati.
16.2.e:
If your ear wanders
among sounds without check,
not seeing the danger,
you’re not freed from suffering.

16.2.s:
Anissaraṇadassāvī,
gandhe ce paṭisevati;
Na so muccati dukkhamhā,
gandhesu adhimucchito.
16.2.e:
If, not seeing the escape,
you indulge in a smell,
you’re not freed from suffering,
being besotted by smells.

16.2.s:
Ambilaṁ madhuraggañca,
tittakaggamanussaraṁ;
Rasataṇhāya gadhito,
hadayaṁ nāvabujjhati.
16.2.e:
Recollecting the sour,
the superbly sweet and the bitter,
captivated by craving for taste,
you don’t understand the heart.

16.2.s:
Subhānyappaṭikūlāni,
phoṭṭhabbāni anussaraṁ;
Ratto rāgādhikaraṇaṁ,
vividhaṁ vindate dukhaṁ.
16.2.e:
Recollecting lovely
and pleasurable touches,
full of desire, you experience
many kinds of suffering because of lust.

16.2.s:
Manaṁ cetehi dhammehi,
yo na sakkoti rakkhituṁ;
Tato naṁ dukkhamanveti,
sabbehetehi pañcahi.
16.2.e:
Unable to protect
the mind from such thoughts,
suffering follows them
because of all five.

16.2.s:
Pubbalohitasampuṇṇaṁ,
bahussa kuṇapassa ca;
Naravīrakataṁ vagguṁ,
samuggamiva cittitaṁ.
16.2.e:
This body is full of pus and blood,
it’s home to many carcasses;
but cunning people decorate it
like a lovely painted casket.

16.2.s:
Kaṭukaṁ madhurassādaṁ,
piyanibandhanaṁ dukhaṁ;
Khuraṁva madhunā littaṁ,
ullihaṁ nāvabujjhati.
16.2.e:
You don’t understand that
the sweetness of honey turns bitter,
and the bonds to those we love cause pain,
like a razor’s edge smeared with honey.

16.2.s:
Itthirūpe itthisare,
phoṭṭhabbepi ca itthiyā;
Itthigandhesu sāratto,
vividhaṁ vindate dukhaṁ.

Itthisotāni sabbāni,
sandanti pañca pañcasu;
Tesamāvaraṇaṁ kātuṁ,
yo sakkoti vīriyavā.
16.2.e:
All of a woman’s streams
flow from five to five.
Whoever, being energetic,
is able to curb these,

16.2.s:
So atthavā so dhammaṭṭho,
so dakkho so vicakkhaṇo;
Kareyya ramamānopi,
kiccaṁ dhammatthasaṁhitaṁ.
16.2.e:
purposeful and firm in principle,
is clever and clear-seeing.
Though he might enjoy himself,
his duty is connected with the teaching and its goal.

16.2.s:
Atho sīdati saññuttaṁ,
vajje kiccaṁ niratthakaṁ;
‘Na taṁ kiccan’ti maññitvā,
appamatto vicakkhaṇo.
16.2.e:
One who’s diligent and discerning,
thinking, ‘This ought not be done’,
would avoid a useless task
that’s doomed to failure.

16.2.s:
Yañca atthena saññuttaṁ,
yā ca dhammagatā rati;
Taṁ samādāya vattetha,
sā hi ve uttamā rati.
16.2.e:
Whatever is meaningful,
and whatever happiness is principled,
let one proceed having undertaken that:
this is the best happiness.

16.2.s:
Uccāvacehupāyehi,
Paresamabhijigīsati;
Hantvā vadhitvā atha socayitvā,
Ālopati sāhasā yo paresaṁ.
16.2.e:
They want to get hold of what belongs to others
by any means, fair or foul.
They kill, injure, and torment,
violently plundering what belongs to others.

16.2.s:
Tacchanto āṇiyā āṇiṁ,
nihanti balavā yathā;
Indriyānindriyeheva,
nihanti kusalo tathā.
16.2.e:
Just as a strong person when building
knocks out a peg with a peg,
so the skillful person
knocks out the faculties with the faculties.

16.2.s:
Saddhaṁ vīriyaṁ samādhiñca,
satipaññañca bhāvayaṁ;
Pañca pañcahi hantvāna,
anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo.
16.2.e:
Developing faith, energy, immersion,
mindfulness, and wisdom;
destroying the five with the five,
the brahmin walks on untroubled.

16.2.s:
So atthavā so dhammaṭṭho,
katvā vākyānusāsaniṁ;
Sabbena sabbaṁ buddhassa,
so naro sukhamedhatī”ti.
16.2.e:
Purposeful and firm in principle,
having fulfilled in every respect
the instructions spoken by the Buddha,
that person prospers in happiness.”

16.3.s:
“Cirarattaṁ vatātāpī,
dhammaṁ anuvicintayaṁ;
Samaṁ cittassa nālatthaṁ,
pucchaṁ samaṇabrāhmaṇe.
16.3.e:
For a long time, sadly,
though I keenly contemplated the teaching,
I gained no peace of mind.
So I asked this of ascetics and brahmins:

16.3.s:
‘Ko so pāraṅgato loke,
ko patto amatogadhaṁ;
Kassa dhammaṁ paṭicchāmi,
paramatthavijānanaṁ’.
16.3.e:
“Who in the world have crossed over?
Whose attainment has freedom from death <j>as its objective?
Whose teaching do I accept
to understand the ultimate goal?

16.3.s:
Antovaṅkagato āsi,
macchova ghasamāmisaṁ;
Baddho mahindapāsena,
vepacityasuro yathā.
16.3.e:
I was hooked inside,
like a fish gulping bait;
bound like the titan Vepaciti
in Mahinda’s trap.

16.3.s:
Añchāmi naṁ na muñcāmi,
asmā sokapariddavā;
Ko me bandhaṁ muñcaṁ loke,
sambodhiṁ vedayissati.
16.3.e:
Dragging it along, I’m not free
from grief and lamentation.
Who will free me from bonds in the world,
so that I may know awakening?

16.3.s:
Samaṇaṁ brāhmaṇaṁ vā kaṁ,
ādisantaṁ pabhaṅgunaṁ;
Kassa dhammaṁ paṭicchāmi,
jarāmaccupavāhanaṁ.
16.3.e:
What ascetic or brahmin
points out what is frail?
Whose teaching do I accept
to rinse off old age and death?

16.3.s:
Vicikicchākaṅkhāganthitaṁ,
sārambhabalasaññutaṁ;
Kodhappattamanatthaddhaṁ,
abhijappappadāraṇaṁ.
16.3.e:
Tied up with uncertainty and doubt,
secured by the power of aggression,
stiff as a mind beset by anger;
the arrow of covetousness,

16.3.s:
Taṇhādhanusamuṭṭhānaṁ,
dve ca pannarasāyutaṁ;
Passa orasikaṁ bāḷhaṁ,
bhetvāna yadi tiṭṭhati.
16.3.e:
propelled by the bow of craving,
is stuck in my twice-fifteen ribcage—
see how it stands in my breast,
breaking my strong heart.

16.3.s:
Anudiṭṭhīnaṁ appahānaṁ,
saṅkappaparatejitaṁ;
Tena viddho pavedhāmi,
pattaṁva māluteritaṁ.
16.3.e:
Theories are not abandoned,
they are sharpened by memories and intentions;
and pierced by this I tremble,
like a leaf blowing in the gale.

16.3.s:
Ajjhattaṁ me samuṭṭhāya,
khippaṁ paccati māmakaṁ;
Chaphassāyatanī kāyo,
yattha sarati sabbadā.
16.3.e:
Having arisen within,
what belongs to me burns quickly,
in that place where the body always heads
with its six sense-fields of contact.

16.3.s:
Taṁ na passāmi tekicchaṁ,
yo metaṁ sallamuddhare;
Nānārajjena satthena,
nāññena vicikicchitaṁ.
16.3.e:
I don’t see a healer
who can pull out my dart of doubt
without a lance
or some other blade.

16.3.s:
Ko me asattho avaṇo,
Sallamabbhantarapassayaṁ;
Ahiṁsaṁ sabbagattāni,
Sallaṁ me uddharissati.
16.3.e:
Without knife or wound,
who will pull out this dart
that’s stuck inside me,
without harming any part of my body?

16.3.s:
Dhammappati hi so seṭṭho,
visadosappavāhako;
Gambhīre patitassa me,
thalaṁ pāṇiñca dassaye.
16.3.e:
He really would be the Lord of the Dhamma,
the best one to cure the damage of poison;
when I have fallen into deep waters,
he would show me his hand and the shore.

16.3.s:
Rahadehamasmi ogāḷho,
ahāriyarajamattike;
Māyāusūyasārambha,
thinamiddhamapatthaṭe.
16.3.e:
I’ve plunged into a lake,
and I can’t wash off the mud and dirt.
It’s full of deceit, jealousy, aggression,
and dullness and drowsiness.

16.3.s:
Uddhaccameghathanitaṁ,
saṁyojanavalāhakaṁ;
Vāhā vahanti kuddiṭṭhiṁ,
saṅkappā rāganissitā.
16.3.e:
Like a thundering cloud of restlessness,
like a stormcloud of fetters;
lustful thoughts are winds
that sweep off a person with bad views.

16.3.s:
Savanti sabbadhi sotā,
latā ubbhijja tiṭṭhati;
Te sote ko nivāreyya,
taṁ lataṁ ko hi checchati.
16.3.e:
The streams flow everywhere;
a weed springs up and remains.
Who will block the streams?
Who will cut the weed?”

16.3.s:
Velaṁ karotha bhaddante,
sotānaṁ sannivāraṇaṁ;
Mā te manomayo soto,
rukkhaṁva sahasā luve.
16.3.e:
“Venerable sir, build a dam
to block the streams.
Don’t let your mind-made streams
cut you down suddenly like a tree.”

16.3.s:
Evaṁ me bhayajātassa,
apārā pāramesato;
Tāṇo paññāvudho satthā,
isisaṅghanisevito.
16.3.e:
That is how, when I was full of fear,
seeking the far shore from the near,
my shelter was the Teacher whose weapon is wisdom,
frequented by the Saṅgha of seers.

16.3.s:
Sopāṇaṁ sugataṁ suddhaṁ,
dhammasāramayaṁ daḷhaṁ;
Pādāsi vuyhamānassa,
‘mā bhāyī’ti ca mabravi.
16.3.e:
As I was being swept away,
he gave me a strong, simple ladder,
made of the heartwood of Dhamma,
and he said to me: “Do not fear.”

16.3.s:
Satipaṭṭhānapāsādaṁ,
āruyha paccavekkhisaṁ;
Yaṁ taṁ pubbe amaññissaṁ,
sakkāyābhirataṁ pajaṁ.
16.3.e:
I climbed the tower of mindfulness meditation,
and checked back down
at people delighting in substantial reality,
as I had obsessed over in the past.

16.3.s:
Yadā ca maggamaddakkhiṁ,
nāvāya abhirūhanaṁ;
Anadhiṭṭhāya attānaṁ,
titthamaddakkhimuttamaṁ.
16.3.e:
When I saw the path,
as I was embarking on the ship,
without fixating on the self,
I saw the supreme landing-place.

16.3.s:
Sallaṁ attasamuṭṭhānaṁ,
bhavanettippabhāvitaṁ;
Etesaṁ appavattāya,
desesi maggamuttamaṁ.
16.3.e:
The dart that arises in oneself,
and that which stems from the leash to existence:
he taught the supreme path
for the canceling of these.

16.3.s:
Dīgharattānusayitaṁ,
cirarattamadhiṭṭhitaṁ;
Buddho mepānudī ganthaṁ,
visadosappavāhano”ti.

16.4.s:
“Passa cittakataṁ bimbaṁ,
arukāyaṁ samussitaṁ;
Āturaṁ bahusaṅkappaṁ,
yassa natthi dhuvaṁ ṭhiti.
16.4.e:
“See this fancy puppet,
a body built of sores,
diseased, obsessed over,
in which nothing lasts at all.

16.4.s:
Passa cittakataṁ rūpaṁ,
maṇinā kuṇḍalena ca;
Aṭṭhiṁ tacena onaddhaṁ,
saha vatthehi sobhati.
16.4.e:
See this fancy figure,
with its gems and earrings;
it is bones swathed in skin,
made pretty by its clothes.

16.4.s:
Alattakakatā pādā,
mukhaṁ cuṇṇakamakkhitaṁ;
Alaṁ bālassa mohāya,
no ca pāragavesino.
16.4.e:
Rouged feet
and powdered face
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.

16.4.s:
Aṭṭhapadakatā kesā,
nettā añjanamakkhitā;
Alaṁ bālassa mohāya,
no ca pāragavesino.
16.4.e:
Hair in eight braids
and eyeshadow
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.

16.4.s:
Añjanīva navā cittā,
pūtikāyo alaṅkato;
Alaṁ bālassa mohāya,
no ca pāragavesino.
16.4.e:
A rotting body all adorned
like a freshly painted makeup box
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.

16.4.s:
Odahi migavo pāsaṁ,
nāsadā vāguraṁ migo;
Bhutvā nivāpaṁ gacchāma,
kandante migabandhake.
16.4.e:
The hunter laid his snare,
but the deer didn’t spring the trap.
I’ve eaten the bait and now I go,
leaving the trapper to lament.

16.4.s:
Chinno pāso migavassa,
nāsadā vāguraṁ migo;
Bhutvā nivāpaṁ gacchāma,
socante migaluddake.
16.4.e:
The hunter’s snare is broken,
but the deer didn’t spring the trap.
I’ve eaten the bait and now I go,
leaving the deer-hunter to grieve.”

16.4.s:
Passāmi loke sadhane manusse,
Laddhāna vittaṁ na dadanti mohā;
Luddhā dhanaṁ sannicayaṁ karonti,
Bhiyyova kāme abhipatthayanti.
16.4.e:
“I see rich people in the world who,
because of delusion, <j>give not the wealth they’ve earned.
Greedily, they hoard their riches,
yearning for ever more sensual pleasures.

16.4.s:
Rājā pasayhappathaviṁ vijetvā,
Sasāgarantaṁ mahimāvasanto;
Oraṁ samuddassa atittarūpo,
Pāraṁ samuddassapi patthayetha.
16.4.e:
A king who conquered the earth by force,
ruling the land from sea to sea,
unsatisfied with the near shore of the ocean,
would still yearn for the further shore.

16.4.s:
Rājā ca aññe ca bahū manussā,
Avītataṇhā maraṇaṁ upenti;
Ūnāva hutvāna jahanti dehaṁ,
Kāmehi lokamhi na hatthi titti.
16.4.e:
Not just the king, but others too,
reach death not rid of craving.
They leave the body still wanting,
for in this world sensual pleasures never satisfy.

16.4.s:
Kandanti naṁ ñātī pakiriya kese,
Aho vatā no amarāti cāhu;
Vatthena naṁ pārutaṁ nīharitvā,
Citaṁ samodhāya tato ḍahanti.
16.4.e:
Relatives lament, their hair disheveled,
saying ‘Ah! Alas! They’re not immortal!’
They take out the body wrapped in a shroud,
heap up a pyre, and burn it there.

16.4.s:
So ḍayhati sūlehi tujjamāno,
Ekena vatthena pahāya bhoge;
Na mīyamānassa bhavanti tāṇā,
Ñātī ca mittā atha vā sahāyā.
16.4.e:
It’s poked with stakes while being burnt,
in just a single cloth, all wealth gone.
Relatives, friends, and companions
can’t help you when you’re dying.

16.4.s:
Dāyādakā tassa dhanaṁ haranti,
Satto pana gacchati yena kammaṁ;
Na mīyamānaṁ dhanamanveti kiñci,
Puttā ca dārā ca dhanañca raṭṭhaṁ.
16.4.e:
Heirs take your riches,
while beings fare on according to their deeds.
Riches don’t follow you when you die;
nor do children, wife, wealth, nor kingdom.

16.4.s:
Na dīghamāyuṁ labhate dhanena,
Na cāpi vittena jaraṁ vihanti;
Appaṁ hidaṁ jīvitamāhu dhīrā,
Asassataṁ vippariṇāmadhammaṁ.

Aḍḍhā daliddā ca phusanti phassaṁ,
Bālo ca dhīro ca tatheva phuṭṭho;
Bālo hi bālyā vadhitova seti,
Dhīro ca no vedhati phassaphuṭṭho.
16.4.e:
The rich and the poor feel its touch;
the fool and the attentive one feel it too.
But the fool lies stricken by their own folly,
while the attentive don’t tremble at the touch.

16.4.s:
Tasmā hi paññāva dhanena seyyā,
Yāya vosānamidhādhigacchati;
Abyositattā hi bhavābhavesu,
Pāpāni kammāni karoti mohā.
16.4.e:
Therefore wisdom’s much better than wealth,
since by wisdom <j>you reach consummation in this life.
But if because of delusion <j>you don’t reach consummation,
you’ll do evil deeds in life after life.

16.4.s:
Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṁ,
Saṁsāramāpajja paramparāya;
Tassappapañño abhisaddahanto,
Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṁ.
16.4.e:
One who enters a womb and the world beyond,
will transmigrate from one life to the next.
While someone of little wisdom, <j>placing faith in them,
also enters a womb and the world beyond.

16.4.s:
Coro yathā sandhimukhe gahīto,
Sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo;
Evaṁ pajā pecca paramhi loke,
Sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo.
16.4.e:
As a bandit caught in a window
is punished for his own bad deeds;
so after departing, in the world beyond,
people are punished for their own bad deeds.

16.4.s:
Kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā,
Virūparūpena mathenti cittaṁ;
Ādīnavaṁ kāmaguṇesu disvā,
Tasmā ahaṁ pabbajitomhi rāja.
16.4.e:
Sensual pleasures are diverse, sweet, delightful;
appearing in disguise they disturb the mind.
Seeing danger in sensual stimulations,
I went forth, O King.

16.4.s:
Dumapphalānīva patanti māṇavā,
Daharā ca vuḍḍhā ca sarīrabhedā;
Etampi disvā pabbajitomhi rāja,
Apaṇṇakaṁ sāmaññameva seyyo.
16.4.e:
As fruit falls from a tree, so the sons of Manu fall,
young and old, when the body breaks up.
Seeing this, too, I went forth, O King;
it’s a sure bet that the ascetic life is better.”

16.4.s:
Saddhāyāhaṁ pabbajito,
upeto jinasāsane;
Avañjhā mayhaṁ pabbajjā,
anaṇo bhuñjāmi bhojanaṁ.
16.4.e:
“I went forth out of faith
joining the victor’s dispensation.
My going forth wasn’t wasted;
I enjoy my food free of debt.

16.4.s:
Kāme ādittato disvā,
Jātarūpāni satthato;
Gabbhavokkantito dukkhaṁ,
Nirayesu mahabbhayaṁ.
16.4.e:
I saw sensual pleasures as burning,
gold as a cutting blade,
conception in a womb as suffering,
and the hells as very fearful.

16.4.s:
Etamādīnavaṁ ñatvā,
saṁvegaṁ alabhiṁ tadā;
Sohaṁ viddho tadā santo,
sampatto āsavakkhayaṁ.
16.4.e:
Knowing this danger,
I was struck with a sense of urgency.
I was stabbed, but then I found peace,
attaining the end of defilements.

16.4.s:
Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā,
kataṁ buddhassa sāsanaṁ;
Ohito garuko bhāro,
bhavanetti samūhatā.
16.4.e:
I’ve served the Teacher
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
The heavy burden is laid down,
the leash to existence is eradicated.

16.4.s:
Yassatthāya pabbajito,
agārasmānagāriyaṁ;
So me attho anuppatto,
sabbasaṁyojanakkhayo”ti.
16.4.e:
I’ve attained the goal
for the sake of which I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness—
the ending of all fetters.”

16.5.s:
“Rūpaṁ disvā sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you see a sight, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from sights.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Saddaṁ sutvā sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you hear a sound, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from sounds.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Gandhaṁ ghatvā sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you smell an odor, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from smells.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Rasaṁ bhotvā sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you enjoy a taste, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from tastes.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Phassaṁ phussa sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you sense a touch, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from touches.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Dhammaṁ ñatvā sati muṭṭhā,
Piyaṁ nimittaṁ manasi karoto;
Sārattacitto vedeti,
Tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
When you know an idea, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.

Many feelings grow
arising from ideas.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati rūpesu,
rūpaṁ disvā patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for sights
when you see a sight with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you see a sight
and undergo a feeling,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati saddesu,
saddaṁ sutvā patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for sounds
when you hear a sound with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you hear a sound
and undergo a feeling,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati gandhesu,
gandhaṁ ghatvā patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for odors
when you smell an odor with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you smell an odor
and undergo a feeling,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati rasesu,
rasaṁ bhotvā patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for tastes
when you enjoy a taste with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you savor a taste
and undergo a feeling,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati phassesu,
phassaṁ phussa patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for touches
when you sense a touch with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you sense a touch
and get familiar with how it feels,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.5.s:
Na so rajjati dhammesu,
dhammaṁ ñatvā patissato;
Virattacitto vedeti,
tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.
16.5.e:
There’s no desire for ideas
when you know an idea with mindfulness.
Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,
you don’t keep clinging to it.

Even as you know an idea
and get familiar with how it feels,
you wear away, you don’t heap up:
that’s how to live mindfully.
Eroding suffering like this,
you’re said to be in the presence of extinguishment.

16.6.s:
“Paripuṇṇakāyo suruci,
Sujāto cārudassano;
Suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā,
Susukkadāṭhosi vīriyavā.
16.6.e:
“O Blessed One, your body’s perfect,
you’re radiant, handsome, lovely to behold;
golden colored,
with teeth so white; you’re strong.

16.6.s:
Narassa hi sujātassa,
ye bhavanti viyañjanā;
Sabbe te tava kāyasmiṁ,
mahāpurisalakkhaṇā.
16.6.e:
The characteristics
of a handsome man,
the marks of a great man,
are all found on your body.

16.6.s:
Pasannanetto sumukho,
brahā uju patāpavā;
Majjhe samaṇasaṅghassa,
ādiccova virocasi.
16.6.e:
Your eyes are clear, your face is fair,
you’re formidable, upright, majestic.
In the midst of the Saṅgha of ascetics,
you dazzle like the sun.

16.6.s:
Kalyāṇadassano bhikkhu,
kañcanasannibhattaco;
Kiṁ te samaṇabhāvena,
evaṁ uttamavaṇṇino.
16.6.e:
You’re a mendicant fine to see,
with skin that shines like lustrous gold.
But with such excellent appearance,
what do you want with the ascetic life?

16.6.s:
Rājā arahasi bhavituṁ,
cakkavattī rathesabho;
Cāturanto vijitāvī,
jambusaṇḍassa issaro.
16.6.e:
You’re fit to be a king,
a wheel-turning monarch, chief of charioteers,
victorious in the four quarters,
lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.

16.6.s:
Khattiyā bhogī rājāno,
anuyantā bhavanti te;
Rājābhirājā manujindo,
rajjaṁ kārehi gotama”.
16.6.e:
Aristocrats, nobles, and kings
ought follow your rule.
Gotama, may you reign
as king of kings, lord of mankind!”

16.6.s:
“Rājāhamasmi sela, (selāti bhagavā)
Dhammarājā anuttaro;
Dhammena cakkaṁ vattemi,
Cakkaṁ appaṭivattiyaṁ”.
16.6.e:
“I am a king, Sela”, said the Buddha to Sela,
“the supreme king of the teaching.
By the teaching I roll forth the wheel
which cannot be rolled back.”

16.6.s:
“Sambuddho paṭijānāsi, (iti selo brāhmaṇo)
Dhammarājā anuttaro;
‘Dhammena cakkaṁ vattemi’,
Iti bhāsatha gotama.
16.6.e:
“You claim to be awakened,” said Sela the brahmin,
“the supreme king of the teaching.
‘I roll forth the teaching’:
so you say, Gotama.

16.6.s:
Ko nu senāpati bhoto,
sāvako satthuranvayo;
Ko tetamanuvatteti,
dhammacakkaṁ pavattitaṁ”.
16.6.e:
Then who is your general,
the disciple who follows the Teacher’s way?
Who keeps rolling the wheel
of the teaching you rolled forth?”

16.6.s:
“Mayā pavattitaṁ cakkaṁ, (selāti bhagavā)
Dhammacakkaṁ anuttaraṁ;
Sāriputto anuvatteti,
Anujāto tathāgataṁ.
16.6.e:
“By me the wheel was rolled forth,” said the Buddha,
“the supreme wheel of the teaching.
Sāriputta, taking after the Realized One,
keeps it rolling on.

16.6.s:
Abhiññeyyaṁ abhiññātaṁ,
bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṁ;
Pahātabbaṁ pahīnaṁ me,
tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa.
16.6.e:
I have known what should be known,
and developed what should be developed,
and given up what should be given up:
and so, brahmin, I am a Buddha.

16.6.s:
Vinayassu mayi kaṅkhaṁ,
adhimuccassu brāhmaṇa;
Dullabhaṁ dassanaṁ hoti,
sambuddhānaṁ abhiṇhaso.
16.6.e:
Dispel your doubt in me—
make up your mind, brahmin!
The sight of a Buddha
is hard to find again.

16.6.s:
Yesaṁ ve dullabho loke,
pātubhāvo abhiṇhaso;
Sohaṁ brāhmaṇa buddhosmi,
sallakatto anuttaro.
16.6.e:
I am a Buddha, brahmin,
the supreme surgeon,
one of those whose appearance in the world
is hard to find again.

16.6.s:
Brahmabhūto atitulo,
mārasenappamaddano;
Sabbāmitte vase katvā,
modāmi akutobhayo”.
16.6.e:
A manifestation of divinity, unequaled,
crusher of Māra’s army;
having subdued all my opponents,
I rejoice, fearing nothing from any quarter.”

16.6.s:
“Idaṁ bhonto nisāmetha,
yathā bhāsati cakkhumā;
Sallakatto mahāvīro,
sīhova nadatī vane.
16.6.e:
“Pay heed, sirs, to what
is spoken by the Clear-eyed One.
The surgeon, the great hero,
roars like a lion in the jungle.

16.6.s:
Brahmabhūtaṁ atitulaṁ,
mārasenappamaddanaṁ;
Ko disvā nappasīdeyya,
api kaṇhābhijātiko.
16.6.e:
A manifestation of divinity, unequaled,
crusher of Māra’s army;
who would not be inspired by him,
even one born in a dark class?

16.6.s:
Yo maṁ icchati anvetu,
yo vā nicchati gacchatu;
Idhāhaṁ pabbajissāmi,
varapaññassa santike”.
16.6.e:
Those who wish may follow me;
those who don’t may go.
Right here, I’ll go forth in his presence,
the one of such outstanding wisdom.”

16.6.s:
“Etañce ruccati bhoto,
sammāsambuddhasāsanaṁ;
Mayampi pabbajissāma,
varapaññassa santike”.
16.6.e:
“Sir, if you endorse
the teaching of the Buddha,
we’ll also go forth in his presence,
the one of such outstanding wisdom.”

16.6.s:
“Brāhmaṇā tisatā ime,
yācanti pañjalīkatā;
‘Brahmacariyaṁ carissāma,
bhagavā tava santike’”.
16.6.e:
“These three hundred brahmins
with cupped palms held up, ask:
‘May we lead the spiritual life
in your presence, Blessed One?’”

16.6.s:
“Svākkhātaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, (selāti bhagavā)
Sandiṭṭhikamakālikaṁ;
Yattha amoghā pabbajjā,
Appamattassa sikkhato”.
16.6.e:
“The spiritual life is well explained,” said the Buddha,
“apparent in the present life, immediately effective.
Here the going forth isn’t in vain
for one who trains with diligence.”

16.6.s:
“Yaṁ taṁ saraṇamāgamha,
ito aṭṭhame cakkhuma;
Sattarattena bhagavā,
dantāmha tava sāsane.
16.6.e:
“This is the eighth day since
we went for refuge, O Clear-eyed One.
In these seven days, Blessed One,
we’ve become tamed in your teaching.

16.6.s:
Tuvaṁ buddho tuvaṁ satthā,
tuvaṁ mārābhibhū muni;
Tuvaṁ anusaye chetvā,
tiṇṇo tāresimaṁ pajaṁ.
16.6.e:
You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher,
you are the sage who has overcome Māra;
you have cut off the underlying tendencies,
you’ve crossed over, and you bring humanity across.

16.6.s:
Upadhī te samatikkantā,
āsavā te padālitā;
Sīhova anupādāno,
pahīnabhayabheravo.
16.6.e:
You have transcended attachments,
your defilements are shattered;
like a lion free of grasping,
with fear and dread given up.

16.6.s:
Bhikkhavo tisatā ime,
tiṭṭhanti pañjalīkatā;
Pāde vīra pasārehi,
nāgā vandantu satthuno”ti.
16.6.e:
These three hundred mendicants
stand with cupped palms raised.
Stretch out your feet, great hero:
let these giants bow to the Teacher.”

16.7.s:
“Yātaṁ me hatthigīvāya,
sukhumā vatthā padhāritā;
Sālīnaṁ odano bhutto,
sucimaṁsūpasecano.
16.7.e:
I rode on an elephant’s neck,
wearing luxurious clothes.
I ate boiled fine rice
with pure meat sauce.

16.7.s:
Sojja bhaddo sātatiko,
uñchāpattāgate rato;
Jhāyati anupādāno,
putto godhāya bhaddiyo.
16.7.e:
Today I am fortunate, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

16.7.s:
Paṁsukūlī sātatiko,
uñchāpattāgate rato;
Jhāyati anupādāno,
putto godhāya bhaddiyo.
16.7.e:
Wearing rags, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Living on almsfood, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Possessing only three robes, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Wandering for alms indiscriminately, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Sitting alone, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Eating only what’s put in the alms-bowl, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Never eating too late, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Living in the wilderness, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Living at the foot of a tree, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Living in the open, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Living in a charnel ground, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Accepting whatever seat is offered, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Not lying down to sleep, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Few in wishes, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Content, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Secluded, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Aloof, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

Energetic, persistent,
happy with the scraps in my bowl:
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
practices absorption without grasping.

16.7.s:
Hitvā satapalaṁ kaṁsaṁ,
sovaṇṇaṁ satarājikaṁ;
Aggahiṁ mattikāpattaṁ,
idaṁ dutiyābhisecanaṁ.
16.7.e:
Giving up a hundred ounces of bronze,
and a hundred grains of gold,
I took a bowl made of clay:
this is my second initiation.

16.7.s:
Ucce maṇḍalipākāre,
daḷhamaṭṭālakoṭṭhake;
Rakkhito khaggahatthehi,
uttasaṁ vihariṁ pure.
16.7.e:
I used to live in a citadel with walls so high,
with battlements strong and gates,
all guarded by swordsmen—
and yet I was afraid.

16.7.s:
Sojja bhaddo anutrāsī,
pahīnabhayabheravo;
Jhāyati vanamoggayha,
putto godhāya bhaddiyo.
16.7.e:
Today I am fortunate, free of cowardice,
with fear and dread given up.
Bhaddiya son of Godhā
has plunged into the forest and practices absorption.

16.7.s:
Sīlakkhandhe patiṭṭhāya,
satiṁ paññañca bhāvayaṁ;
Pāpuṇiṁ anupubbena,
sabbasaṁyojanakkhayan”ti.
16.7.e:
Established in the entire spectrum of ethics,
developing mindfulness and wisdom,
gradually I attained
the ending of all fetters.

16.8.s:
“Gacchaṁ vadesi samaṇaṭṭhitomhi,
Mamañca brūsi ṭhitamaṭṭhitoti;
Pucchāmi taṁ samaṇa etamatthaṁ,
‘Kathaṁ ṭhito tvaṁ ahamaṭṭhitomhi’”.
16.8.e:
“While walking, ascetic, you say ‘I’ve stopped.’
And I have stopped, but you tell me I’ve not.
I’m asking you this, ascetic:
how is it you’ve stopped and I have not?”

16.8.s:
“Ṭhito ahaṁ aṅgulimāla sabbadā,
Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṁ;
Tuvañca pāṇesu asaññatosi,
Tasmā ṭhitohaṁ tuvamaṭṭhitosi”.
16.8.e:
“Aṅgulimāla, I have forever stopped—
I’ve laid aside violence toward all creatures.
But you can’t stop yourself <j>from harming living creatures;
that’s why I’ve stopped, but you have not.”

16.8.s:
“Cirassaṁ vata me mahito mahesī,
Mahāvanaṁ samaṇo paccapādi;
Sohaṁ cajissāmi sahassapāpaṁ,
Sutvāna gāthaṁ tava dhammayuttaṁ”.
16.8.e:
“Oh, at long last a renowned great seer,
an ascetic has followed me into this deep wood.
Now that I’ve heard your verse on Dhamma,
I shall discard a thousand evils.”

16.8.s:
Icceva coro asimāvudhañca,
Sobbhe papāte narake anvakāsi;
Avandi coro sugatassa pāde,
Tattheva pabbajjamayāci buddhaṁ.
16.8.e:
With these words, <j>the bandit hurled his sword and weapons
down a cliff into an abyss.
He venerated the Holy One’s feet,
and requested the going forth <j>from the Buddha right away.

16.8.s:
Buddho ca kho kāruṇiko mahesi,
Yo satthā lokassa sadevakassa;
“Tamehi bhikkhū”ti tadā avoca,
Eseva tassa ahu bhikkhubhāvo.
16.8.e:
Then the Buddha, the compassionate great seer,
the Teacher of the world with its gods,
said to him, “Come, monk!”
And with that he became a monk.

16.8.s:
“Yo ca pubbe pamajjitvā,
pacchā so nappamajjati;
Somaṁ lokaṁ pabhāseti,
abbhā muttova candimā.
16.8.e:
“He who once was heedless,
but turned to heedfulness,
shines upon this world,
like the moon freed from clouds.

16.8.s:
Yassa pāpaṁ kataṁ kammaṁ,
kusalena pidhīyati;
Somaṁ lokaṁ pabhāseti,
abbhā muttova candimā.
16.8.e:
Someone whose bad deed
is supplanted by the good,
shines upon this world,
like the moon freed from clouds.

16.8.s:
Yo have daharo bhikkhu,
yuñjati buddhasāsane;
Somaṁ lokaṁ pabhāseti,
abbhā muttova candimā.
16.8.e:
A young mendicant
devoted to the Buddha’s teaching,
shines upon this world,
like the moon freed from clouds.

16.8.s:
Disāpi me dhammakathaṁ suṇantu,
Disāpi me yuñjantu buddhasāsane;
Disāpi me te manuje bhajantu,
Ye dhammamevādapayanti santo.
16.8.e:
May even my enemies <j>hear a Dhamma talk!
May even my enemies <j>devote themselves to the Buddha’s teaching!
May even my enemies associate with those good men
who establish others in the Dhamma!

16.8.s:
Disā hi me khantivādānaṁ,
avirodhappasaṁsinaṁ;
Suṇantu dhammaṁ kālena,
tañca anuvidhīyantu.

Na hi jātu so mamaṁ hiṁse,
aññaṁ vā pana kiñcanaṁ;
Pappuyya paramaṁ santiṁ,
rakkheyya tasathāvare.
16.8.e:
For then they’d never wish harm
upon myself or others.
Having arrived at ultimate peace,
they’d look after creatures firm and frail.

16.8.s:
Udakañhi nayanti nettikā,
Usukārā namayanti tejanaṁ;
Dāruṁ namayanti tacchakā,
Attānaṁ damayanti paṇḍitā.
16.8.e:
For while irrigators guide water,
fletchers bend arrows straight,
and carpenters bend timber straight,
the astute tame themselves.

16.8.s:
Daṇḍeneke damayanti,
aṅkusebhi kasāhi ca;
Adaṇḍena asatthena,
ahaṁ dantomhi tādinā.
16.8.e:
Some tame by using the rod,
some with goads, and some with whips.
But the unaffected one tamed me
without rod or sword.

16.8.s:
‘Ahiṁsako’ti me nāmaṁ,
hiṁsakassa pure sato;
Ajjāhaṁ saccanāmomhi,
na naṁ hiṁsāmi kiñcanaṁ.
16.8.e:
My name is ‘Harmless’,
though I used to be harmful.
The name I bear today is true,
for I do no harm to anyone.

16.8.s:
Coro ahaṁ pure āsiṁ,
aṅgulimāloti vissuto;
Vuyhamāno mahoghena,
buddhaṁ saraṇamāgamaṁ.
16.8.e:
I used to be a bandit,
the notorious Aṅgulimāla.
Swept away in a great flood,
I went to the Buddha for refuge.

16.8.s:
Lohitapāṇi pure āsiṁ,
aṅgulimāloti vissuto;
Saraṇagamanaṁ passa,
bhavanetti samūhatā.
16.8.e:
I used to have blood on my hands,
the notorious Aṅgulimāla.
See the refuge I’ve found—
the leash to existence is eradicated.

16.8.s:
Tādisaṁ kammaṁ katvāna,
bahuṁ duggatigāminaṁ;
Phuṭṭho kammavipākena,
anaṇo bhuñjāmi bhojanaṁ.
16.8.e:
I’ve done many of the sort of deeds
that lead to a bad destination.
The result of my deeds has already struck me,
so I enjoy my food free of debt.

16.8.s:
Pamādamanuyuñjanti,
bālā dummedhino janā;
Appamādañca medhāvī,
dhanaṁ seṭṭhaṁva rakkhati.
16.8.e:
Fools and simpletons
devote themselves to negligence.
But the wise protect diligence
as their best treasure.

16.8.s:
Mā pamādamanuyuñjetha,
mā kāmaratisanthavaṁ;
Appamatto hi jhāyanto,
pappoti paramaṁ sukhaṁ.
16.8.e:
Don’t devote yourself to negligence,
or delight in erotic intimacy.
For if you’re diligent and practice absorption,
you’ll attain ultimate happiness.

16.8.s:
Svāgataṁ nāpagataṁ,
netaṁ dummantitaṁ mama;
Savibhattesu dhammesu,
yaṁ seṭṭhaṁ tadupāgamaṁ.
16.8.e:
It was welcome, not unwelcome,
the advice I got was good.
Of the well-explained teachings,
I arrived at the best.

16.8.s:
Svāgataṁ nāpagataṁ,
netaṁ dummantitaṁ mama;
Tisso vijjā anuppattā,
kataṁ buddhassa sāsanaṁ.
16.8.e:
It was welcome, not unwelcome,
the advice I got was good.
I’ve attained the three knowledges,
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.”

16.8.s:
Araññe rukkhamūle vā,
pabbatesu guhāsu vā;
Tattha tattheva aṭṭhāsiṁ,
ubbiggamanaso tadā.
16.8.e:
“In the wilderness, at a tree’s root,
on mountains, or in caves—
it used to be that wherever I stood,
my mind was anxious.

16.8.s:
Sukhaṁ sayāmi ṭhāyāmi,
sukhaṁ kappemi jīvitaṁ;
Ahatthapāso mārassa,
aho satthānukampito.
16.8.e:
But now I lie down happily and stand up happily,
I live my life happily,
out of Māra’s reach;
the Teacher had sympathy for me.

16.8.s:
Brahmajacco pure āsiṁ,
udicco ubhato ahu;
Sojja putto sugatassa,
dhammarājassa satthuno.
16.8.e:
I used to be of brahmin birth,
highborn on both sides,
now I’m a son of the Holy One,
the Teacher, King of Dhamma.

16.8.s:
Vītataṇho anādāno,
guttadvāro susaṁvuto;
Aghamūlaṁ vadhitvāna,
patto me āsavakkhayo.
16.8.e:
I am rid of craving, free of grasping,
my sense doors are guarded and well-restrained.
I’ve destroyed the root of gloom,
and attained the ending of defilements.

16.8.s:
Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā,
kataṁ buddhassa sāsanaṁ;
Ohito garuko bhāro,
bhavanetti samūhatā”ti.
16.8.e:
I’ve served the Teacher
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
The heavy burden is laid down,
the leash to existence is eradicated.”

16.9.s:
“Pahāya mātāpitaro,
bhaginī ñātibhātaro;
Pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā,
anuruddhova jhāyati.
16.9.e:
Leaving my mother and father behind,
as well as sisters, kinsmen, and brothers;
having given up the five sensual stimuli,
Anuruddha practices absorption.

16.9.s:
Sameto naccagītehi,
sammatāḷappabodhano;
Na tena suddhimajjhagaṁ,
mārassa visaye rato.
16.9.e:
Surrounded by song and dance,
awakened by cymbals and gongs,
he did not find purification
while delighting in Māra’s domain.

16.9.s:
Etañca samatikkamma,
rato buddhassa sāsane;
Sabboghaṁ samatikkamma,
anuruddhova jhāyati.
16.9.e:
But he has gone beyond all that,
and delights in the Buddha’s teaching.
Having crossed over the entire flood,
Anuruddha practices absorption.

16.9.s:
Rūpā saddā rasā gandhā,
phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā;
Ete ca samatikkamma,
anuruddhova jhāyati.
16.9.e:
Sights, sounds, tastes, smells,
and touches so delightful:
having crossed over these as well,
Anuruddha practices absorption.

16.9.s:
Piṇḍapātamatikkanto,
eko adutiyo muni;
Esati paṁsukūlāni,
anuruddho anāsavo.
16.9.e:
Returning from almsround,
alone, without partner,
seeking rags from the dust heap,
Anuruddha is without defilements.

16.9.s:
Vicinī aggahī dhovi,
rajayī dhārayī muni;
Paṁsukūlāni matimā,
anuruddho anāsavo.

Mahiccho ca asantuṭṭho,
saṁsaṭṭho yo ca uddhato;
Tassa dhammā ime honti,
pāpakā saṅkilesikā.
16.9.e:
The principles of someone
who has many wishes and is not content,
who socializes and is conceited,
are wicked and corrupting.

16.9.s:
Sato ca hoti appiccho,
santuṭṭho avighātavā;
Pavivekarato vitto,
niccamāraddhavīriyo.
16.9.e:
But someone who is mindful, few of wishes,
content and untroubled,
delighting in seclusion, joyful,
always resolute and energetic;

16.9.s:
Tassa dhammā ime honti,
kusalā bodhipakkhikā;
Anāsavo ca so hoti,
iti vuttaṁ mahesinā.
16.9.e:
their principles are skillful,
on the side of awakening;
they are without defilements—
so said the great seer.

16.9.s:
Mama saṅkappamaññāya,
satthā loke anuttaro;
Manomayena kāyena,
iddhiyā upasaṅkami.
16.9.e:
“Knowing my thoughts,
the supreme Teacher in the world
came to me in a mind-made body,
using his psychic power.

16.9.s:
Yadā me ahu saṅkappo,
tato uttari desayi;
Nippapañcarato buddho,
nippapañcamadesayi.
16.9.e:
He taught me more
than I had thought of.
The Buddha who loves non-proliferation
taught me non-proliferation.

16.9.s:
Tassāhaṁ dhammamaññāya,
vihāsiṁ sāsane rato;
Tisso vijjā anuppattā,
kataṁ buddhassa sāsanaṁ.
16.9.e:
Understanding that teaching,
I happily did his bidding.
I’ve attained the three knowledges,
and have fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.

16.9.s:
Pañcapaññāsavassāni,
yato nesajjiko ahaṁ;
Pañcavīsativassāni,
yato middhaṁ samūhataṁ.
16.9.e:
For the last fifty-five years
I have not lain down to sleep.
Twenty-five years have passed
since I eradicated drowsiness.”

16.9.s:
Nāhu assāsapassāsā,
ṭhitacittassa tādino;
Anejo santimārabbha,
cakkhumā parinibbuto.
16.9.e:
“There was no more breathing
for the unaffected one of steady heart.
Imperturbable, committed to peace,
the Clear-eyed One was fully quenched.

16.9.s:
Asallīnena cittena,
vedanaṁ ajjhavāsayi;
Pajjotasseva nibbānaṁ,
vimokkho cetaso ahu.
16.9.e:
He put up with painful feelings
without flinching.
The liberation of his heart
was like the extinguishing of a lamp.”

16.9.s:
Ete pacchimakā dāni,
munino phassapañcamā;
Nāññe dhammā bhavissanti,
sambuddhe parinibbute.
16.9.e:
“Now these touches and the other four
are the last to be experienced by the sage;
nor will there be other phenomena
since the Buddha was fully quenched.

16.9.s:
Natthi dāni punāvāso,
devakāyasmi jālini;
Vikkhīṇo jātisaṁsāro,
natthi dāni punabbhavo.
16.9.e:
O Penelope, weaver of the web—
there’s no more abodes in the heavenly host.
Transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.”

16.9.s:
Yassa muhuttena sahassadhā,
Loko saṁvidito sabrahmakappo;
Vasī iddhiguṇe cutūpapāte,
Kāle passati devatā sa bhikkhu.
16.9.e:
“The mendicant by whom the galaxy
with the age of the Divinity are known in an hour—
that master of psychic ability sees the gods
at the time they pass away and are reborn.”

16.9.s:
Annabhāro pure āsiṁ,
daliddo ghāsahārako;
Samaṇaṁ paṭipādesiṁ,
upariṭṭhaṁ yasassinaṁ.
16.9.e:
“In the past I was Annabhāra,
a poor carrier of fodder.
I practiced as an ascetic,
the renowned Upariṭṭha.

16.9.s:
Somhi sakyakule jāto,
anuruddhoti maṁ vidū;
Upeto naccagītehi,
sammatāḷappabodhano.
16.9.e:
Then I was reborn in the Sakyan clan,
where I was known as ‘Anuruddha’.
Surrounded by song and dance,
I was awakened by cymbals and gongs.

16.9.s:
Athaddasāsiṁ sambuddhaṁ,
satthāraṁ akutobhayaṁ;
Tasmiṁ cittaṁ pasādetvā,
pabbajiṁ anagāriyaṁ.
16.9.e:
Then I saw the Buddha,
the Teacher, fearing nothing from any quarter;
filling my mind with confidence in him,
I went forth to homelessness.

16.9.s:
Pubbenivāsaṁ jānāmi,
yattha me vusitaṁ pure;
Tāvatiṁsesu devesu,
aṭṭhāsiṁ sakkajātiyā.
16.9.e:
I know my past lives,
the places I used to live.
I was born as Sakka,
and stayed among the thirty-three gods.

Seven times I was a king of men
ruling a kingdom,
victorious in the four quarters,
lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.
Without rod or sword,
I governed by principle.

16.9.s:
Ito satta tato satta,
saṁsārāni catuddasa;
Nivāsamabhijānissaṁ,
devaloke ṭhito tadā.
16.9.e:
Seven from here, seven from there—
fourteen transmigrations in all.
I shall remember my past lives:
at that time I stayed in the realm of the gods.

16.9.s:
Pañcaṅgike samādhimhi,
sante ekodibhāvite;
Paṭippassaddhiladdhamhi,
dibbacakkhu visujjhi me.
16.9.e:
I have gained complete tranquility
in immersion with five factors.
Peaceful, serene,
my clairvoyance is purified.

16.9.s:
Cutūpapātaṁ jānāmi,
sattānaṁ āgatiṁ gatiṁ;
Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṁ,
jhāne pañcaṅgike ṭhito.
16.9.e:
Steady in five-factored absorption,
I know the passing away and rebirth of beings,
their coming and going,
their lives in this state and that.

16.9.s:
Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā,
… pe
…
bhavanetti samūhatā.
16.9.e:
I’ve served the Teacher
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
The heavy burden is laid down,
the leash to existence is eradicated.

16.9.s:
Vajjīnaṁ veḷuvagāme,
ahaṁ jīvitasaṅkhayā;
Heṭṭhato veḷugumbasmiṁ,
nibbāyissaṁ anāsavo”ti.
16.9.e:
In the Vajjian village of Veḷuva,
my life will come to an end.
Beneath a thicket of bamboos,
being undefiled, I will be fully extinguished.”

16.10.s:
Samaṇassa ahu cintā,
pupphitamhi mahāvane;
Ekaggassa nisinnassa,
pavivittassa jhāyino.
16.10.e:
This thought came to the ascetic
in the forest full of flowers,
as he was seated alone
meditating in seclusion:

16.10.s:
“Aññathā lokanāthamhi,
tiṭṭhante purisuttame;
Iriyaṁ āsi bhikkhūnaṁ,
aññathā dāni dissati.
16.10.e:
“The behavior of the mendicants
these days seems different
from when the protector of the world,
the best of men, was still here.

16.10.s:
Sītavātaparittāṇaṁ,
hirikopīnachādanaṁ;
Mattaṭṭhiyaṁ abhuñjiṁsu,
santuṭṭhā itarītare.
16.10.e:
Their robes were only for covering the private parts,
and protection from the cold and wind.
They ate in moderation,
content with whatever they were offered.

16.10.s:
Paṇītaṁ yadi vā lūkhaṁ,
appaṁ vā yadi vā bahuṁ;
Yāpanatthaṁ abhuñjiṁsu,
agiddhā nādhimucchitā.
16.10.e:
Whether food was fine or coarse,
a little or a lot,
they ate only for sustenance,
without greed or gluttony.

16.10.s:
Jīvitānaṁ parikkhāre,
bhesajje atha paccaye;
Na bāḷhaṁ ussukā āsuṁ,
yathā te āsavakkhaye.
16.10.e:
They weren’t so very eager
for the requisites of life,
such as tonics and other necessities,
as they were for the ending of defilements.

16.10.s:
Araññe rukkhamūlesu,
kandarāsu guhāsu ca;
Vivekamanubrūhantā,
vihaṁsu tapparāyaṇā.
16.10.e:
In the wilderness, at a tree’s root,
in caves and caverns,
fostering seclusion,
they lived with that as their final goal.

16.10.s:
Nīcā niviṭṭhā subharā,
mudū atthaddhamānasā;
Abyāsekā amukharā,
atthacintā vasānugā.
16.10.e:
They were used to simple things, unburdensome,
gentle, not pompous at heart,
unsullied, not scurrilous,
their thoughts were intent on the goal.

16.10.s:
Tato pāsādikaṁ āsi,
gataṁ bhuttaṁ nisevitaṁ;
Siniddhā teladhārāva,
ahosi iriyāpatho.
16.10.e:
That’s why they inspired confidence,
in their movements, eating, and practice;
their deportment was as smooth
as a stream of oil.

16.10.s:
Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇā,
mahājhāyī mahāhitā;
Nibbutā dāni te therā,
parittā dāni tādisā.
16.10.e:
With the utter ending of all defilements,
those senior monks have now been quenched.
They were great meditators and great benefactors—
there are few like them today.

16.10.s:
Kusalānañca dhammānaṁ,
paññāya ca parikkhayā;
Sabbākāravarūpetaṁ,
lujjate jinasāsanaṁ.
16.10.e:
With the ending
of good principles and understanding,
the victor’s teaching,
full of all excellent qualities, falls apart.

16.10.s:
Pāpakānañca dhammānaṁ,
kilesānañca yo utu;
Upaṭṭhitā vivekāya,
ye ca saddhammasesakā.
16.10.e:
This is the season
for bad principles and defilements.
Those who are ready for seclusion
are all that’s left of the true Dhamma.

16.10.s:
Te kilesā pavaḍḍhantā,
āvisanti bahuṁ janaṁ;
Kīḷanti maññe bālehi,
ummattehiva rakkhasā.
16.10.e:
As they grow, the defilements
possess most people;
they play with fools, it seems to me,
like monsters with the mad.

16.10.s:
Kilesehābhibhūtā te,
tena tena vidhāvitā;
Narā kilesavatthūsu,
sasaṅgāmeva ghosite.
16.10.e:
Overcome by defilements,
they run here and there
among the bases for defilement,
as if they had declared war on themselves.

16.10.s:
Pariccajitvā saddhammaṁ,
aññamaññehi bhaṇḍare;
Diṭṭhigatāni anventā,
idaṁ seyyoti maññare.
16.10.e:
Having forsaken the true teaching,
they argue with each other.
Following wrong views
they think, ‘This is better.’

16.10.s:
Dhanañca puttaṁ bhariyañca,
chaḍḍayitvāna niggatā;
Kaṭacchubhikkhahetūpi,
akicchāni nisevare.
16.10.e:
They cut off their wealth,
children, and wife to go forth.
But then they do what they shouldn’t,
for the sake of a measly spoon of almsfood.

16.10.s:
Udarāvadehakaṁ bhutvā,
sayantuttānaseyyakā;
Kathaṁ vattenti paṭibuddhā,
yā kathā satthugarahitā.
16.10.e:
They eat until their bellies are full,
and then they lie to sleep on their backs.
When they wake up, they keep on chatting,
the kind of talk the Teacher criticized.

16.10.s:
Sabbakārukasippāni,
cittiṁ katvāna sikkhare;
Avūpasantā ajjhattaṁ,
sāmaññatthotiacchati.
16.10.e:
Valuing all the arts and crafts,
they train themselves in them.
Not being settled internally, they think,
‘This is the goal of the ascetic life.’

16.10.s:
Mattikaṁ telacuṇṇañca,
udakāsanabhojanaṁ;
Gihīnaṁ upanāmenti,
ākaṅkhantā bahuttaraṁ.
16.10.e:
They provide clay, oil, and talcum powder,
water, lodgings, and food
for householders,
expecting more in return.

16.10.s:
Dantaponaṁ kapitthañca,
pupphaṁ khādaniyāni ca;
Piṇḍapāte ca sampanne,
ambe āmalakāni ca.
16.10.e:
And in addition, tooth-picks of white fig,
flowers, food to eat,
well-cooked almsfood,
mangoes and myrobalans.

16.10.s:
Bhesajjesu yathā vejjā,
kiccākicce yathā gihī;
Gaṇikāva vibhūsāyaṁ,
issare khattiyā yathā.
16.10.e:
In medicine they are like doctors,
in business like householders,
in makeup like prostitutes,
in sovereignty like aristocrats.

16.10.s:
Nekatikā vañcanikā,
kūṭasakkhī apāṭukā;
Bahūhi parikappehi,
āmisaṁ paribhuñjare.
16.10.e:
Cheats, frauds,
false witnesses, sly:
using multiple plans,
they enjoy things of the flesh.

16.10.s:
Lesakappe pariyāye,
parikappenudhāvitā;
Jīvikatthā upāyena,
saṅkaḍḍhanti bahuṁ dhanaṁ.
16.10.e:
Pursuing shams, contrivances, and plans,
by such means
they accumulate a lot of wealth
for the sake of their own livelihood.

16.10.s:
Upaṭṭhāpenti parisaṁ,
kammato no ca dhammato;
Dhammaṁ paresaṁ desenti,
lābhato no ca atthato.
16.10.e:
They assemble the community
for business rather than Dhamma.
They teach the Dhamma to others
for gain, not for the goal.

16.10.s:
Saṅghalābhassa bhaṇḍanti,
saṅghato paribāhirā;
Paralābhopajīvantā,
ahirīkā na lajjare.
16.10.e:
Those barred from the Saṅgha
quarrel over the Saṅgha’s property.
Lacking conscience, they do not care
that they live on the earnings of others.

16.10.s:
Nānuyuttā tathā eke,
muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā;
Sambhāvanaṁyevicchanti,
lābhasakkāramucchitā.
16.10.e:
Some with shaven head and robe
are not devoted to practice,
but wish only to be honored,
besotted with property and reverence.

16.10.s:
Evaṁ nānappayātamhi,
na dāni sukaraṁ tathā;
Aphusitaṁ vā phusituṁ,
phusitaṁ vānurakkhituṁ.
16.10.e:
When things have come to this,
it’s not easy these days
to realize what has not yet been realized,
or to preserve what has been realized.

16.10.s:
Yathā kaṇṭakaṭṭhānamhi,
careyya anupāhano;
Satiṁ upaṭṭhapetvāna,
evaṁ gāme munī care.
16.10.e:
When shoeless on a thorny path,
one would walk
very mindfully;
that’s how a sage should walk in the village.

16.10.s:
Saritvā pubbake yogī,
tesaṁ vattamanussaraṁ;
Kiñcāpi pacchimo kālo,
phuseyya amataṁ padaṁ.
16.10.e:
Remembering the meditators of old,
and recollecting their conduct,
even in the latter days,
it’s still possible to realize freedom from death.”

16.10.s:
Idaṁ vatvā sālavane,
samaṇo bhāvitindriyo;
Brāhmaṇo parinibbāyī,
isi khīṇapunabbhavo”ti.
16.10.e:
That is what the ascetic, whose faculties
were fully developed, said in the sāl tree grove.
The brahmin, the seer, became fully extinguished,
putting an end to all future lives.

17.1.s:
Pāsādike bahū disvā,
bhāvitatte susaṁvute;
Isi paṇḍarasagotto,
apucchi phussasavhayaṁ.
17.1.e:
Seeing many who inspire confidence,
evolved and well-restrained,
the seer of the Paṇḍara clan,
asked the one known as Phussa:

17.1.s:
“Kiṁchandā kimadhippāyā,
kimākappā bhavissare;
Anāgatamhi kālamhi,
taṁ me akkhāhi pucchito”.
17.1.e:
“In future times,
what desire and motivation
and behavior will people have?
Please answer my question.”

17.1.s:
“Suṇohi vacanaṁ mayhaṁ,
isipaṇḍarasavhaya;
Sakkaccaṁ upadhārehi,
ācikkhissāmyanāgataṁ.
17.1.e:
“Listen to my words,
O seer known as a Paṇḍara,
and remember them carefully,
I will describe the future.

17.1.s:
Kodhanā upanāhī ca,
makkhī thambhī saṭhā bahū;
Ussukī nānāvādā ca,
bhavissanti anāgate.
17.1.e:
In the future many will be
angry and hostile,
offensive, stubborn, and devious,
jealous, holding divergent views.

17.1.s:
Aññātamānino dhamme,
gambhīre tīragocarā;
Lahukā agarū dhamme,
aññamaññamagāravā.
17.1.e:
Imagining they understand <j>the depths of the teaching,
they resort to the near shore.
Superficial and disrespectful toward the teaching,
they lack respect for one another.

17.1.s:
Bahū ādīnavā loke,
uppajjissantyanāgate;
Sudesitaṁ imaṁ dhammaṁ,
kilesessanti dummatī.
17.1.e:
In the future
many dangers will arise in the world.
Idiots will defile
the Dhamma that was taught so well.

17.1.s:
Guṇahīnāpi saṅghamhi,
voharantā visāradā;
Balavanto bhavissanti,
mukharā assutāvino.
17.1.e:
Though bereft of good qualities,
unlearned prattlers, too sure of themselves,
will become powerful
in running Saṅgha proceedings.

17.1.s:
Guṇavantopi saṅghamhi,
voharantā yathātthato;
Dubbalā te bhavissanti,
hirīmanā anatthikā.
17.1.e:
Though possessing good qualities,
the conscientious and unbiased, <j>acting in the proper spirit,
will become weak
in running Saṅgha proceedings.

17.1.s:
Rajataṁ jātarūpañca,
khettaṁ vatthumajeḷakaṁ;
Dāsidāsañca dummedhā,
sādiyissantyanāgate.
17.1.e:
In the future, simpletons will accept
currency and gold,
fields and land, goats and sheep,
and bonded servants, male and female.

17.1.s:
Ujjhānasaññino bālā,
sīlesu asamāhitā;
Unnaḷā vicarissanti,
kalahābhiratā magā.
17.1.e:
Fools finding fault in others,
but unsteady in their own ethics,
will wander about, insolent,
like cantankerous beasts.

17.1.s:
Uddhatā ca bhavissanti,
nīlacīvarapārutā;
Kuhā thaddhā lapā siṅgī,
carissantyariyā viya.
17.1.e:
They’ll be haughty,
wrapped in robes of blue;
deceivers and flatterers, pompous and fake,
they’ll wander as if they were noble ones.

17.1.s:
Telasaṇṭhehi kesehi,
capalā añjanakkhikā;
Rathiyāya gamissanti,
dantavaṇṇikapārutā.
17.1.e:
With hair sleeked back with oil,
fickle, their eyes painted with eyeshadow,
they’ll travel on the high-road,
wrapped in robes of ivory color.

17.1.s:
Ajegucchaṁ vimuttehi,
surattaṁ arahaddhajaṁ;
Jigucchissanti kāsāvaṁ,
odātesu samucchitā.
17.1.e:
The deep-dyed ocher robe,
worn without disgust by the free,
they will come to loathe,
besotted by white clothes.

17.1.s:
Lābhakāmā bhavissanti,
kusītā hīnavīriyā;
Kicchantā vanapatthāni,
gāmantesu vasissare.
17.1.e:
They’ll want lots of possessions,
and be lazy, lacking energy.
Weary of the forest,
they’ll stay within villages.

17.1.s:
Ye ye lābhaṁ labhissanti,
micchājīvaratā sadā;
Te teva anusikkhantā,
bhajissanti asaṁyatā.
17.1.e:
Being unrestrained, they’ll keep company with
those who acquire profit,
and who always enjoy wrong livelihood,
following their example.

17.1.s:
Ye ye alābhino lābhaṁ,
na te pujjā bhavissare;
Supesalepi te dhīre,
sevissanti na te tadā.
17.1.e:
They won’t respect those
who don’t get lots of stuff,
and they won’t associate with the attentive,
even though they’re very amiable.

17.1.s:
Milakkhurajanaṁ rattaṁ,
garahantā sakaṁ dhajaṁ;
Titthiyānaṁ dhajaṁ keci,
dhārissantyavadātakaṁ.
17.1.e:
Disparaging their own banner,
dyed a vermilion color,
some will wear the white banner
of those of other religions.

17.1.s:
Agāravo ca kāsāve,
tadā tesaṁ bhavissati;
Paṭisaṅkhā ca kāsāve,
bhikkhūnaṁ na bhavissati.
17.1.e:
Then they’ll have no respect
for the ocher robe.
The mendicants will not reflect
on the nature of the ocher robe.

17.1.s:
Abhibhūtassa dukkhena,
sallaviddhassa ruppato;
Paṭisaṅkhā mahāghorā,
nāgassāsi acintiyā.
17.1.e:
This awful lack of reflection
was unthinkable to the elephant,
who was overcome by suffering,
inflicted by an arrow strike.

17.1.s:
Chaddanto hi tadā disvā,
surattaṁ arahaddhajaṁ;
Tāvadeva bhaṇī gāthā,
gajo atthopasaṁhitā.
17.1.e:
Then the six-tusked elephant,
seeing the deep-dyed banner of the perfected ones,
straight away spoke these verses
connected with the goal.

17.1.s:
‘Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṁ,
yo vatthaṁ paridhassati;
Apeto damasaccena,
na so kāsāvamarahati.
17.1.e:
‘One who, not free of stains themselves,
would wear the robe stained in ocher,
bereft of self-control and truth:
they are not worthy of the ocher robe.

17.1.s:
Yo ca vantakasāvassa,
sīlesu susamāhito;
Upeto damasaccena,
sa ve kāsāvamarahati.
17.1.e:
One who’s purged all their stains,
steady in ethics,
possessing truth and self-control:
they are truly worthy of the ocher robe.’

17.1.s:
Vipannasīlo dummedho,
pākaṭo kāmakāriyo;
Vibbhantacitto nissukko,
na so kāsāvamarahati.
17.1.e:
Devoid of virtue, a simpleton,
wild, doing what they like,
their minds astray, indolent:
they are not worthy of the ocher robe.

17.1.s:
Yo ca sīlena sampanno,
vītarāgo samāhito;
Odātamanasaṅkappo,
sa ve kāsāvamarahati.
17.1.e:
One accomplished in ethics,
free of greed, serene,
their heart’s intention pure:
they are truly worthy of the ocher robe.

17.1.s:
Uddhato unnaḷo bālo,
sīlaṁ yassa na vijjati;
Odātakaṁ arahati,
kāsāvaṁ kiṁ karissati.
17.1.e:
The haughty, insolent fool,
who has no ethics at all,
is worthy of a white robe—
what use is an ocher robe for them?

17.1.s:
Bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo ca,
duṭṭhacittā anādarā;
Tādīnaṁ mettacittānaṁ,
niggaṇhissantyanāgate.
17.1.e:
In the future, monks and nuns
with corrupt hearts, lacking regard for others,
will disparage those
with hearts of loving-kindness.

17.1.s:
Sikkhāpentāpi therehi,
bālā cīvaradhāraṇaṁ;
Na suṇissanti dummedhā,
pākaṭā kāmakāriyā.
17.1.e:
Though trained in wearing the robe
by senior monks,
simpletons will not listen,
wild, doing what they like.

17.1.s:
Te tathā sikkhitā bālā,
aññamaññaṁ agāravā;
Nādiyissantupajjhāye,
khaḷuṅko viya sārathiṁ.
17.1.e:
With that kind of attitude to training,
those fools won’t respect each other,
or take any notice of their mentors,
like a wild colt with its charioteer.

17.1.s:
Evaṁ anāgataddhānaṁ,
paṭipatti bhavissati;
Bhikkhūnaṁ bhikkhunīnañca,
patte kālamhi pacchime.’
17.1.e:
Even so, in the future,
this will be the practice
of monks and nuns
when the latter days have come.

17.1.s:
Purā āgacchate etaṁ,
anāgataṁ mahabbhayaṁ;
Subbacā hotha sakhilā,
aññamaññaṁ sagāravā.
17.1.e:
Before this frightening future arrives,
be easy to admonish,
courteous in speech,
and respect one another.

17.1.s:
Mettacittā kāruṇikā,
Hotha sīlesu saṁvutā;
Āraddhavīriyā pahitattā,
Niccaṁ daḷhaparakkamā.
17.1.e:
Have hearts of love and compassion,
and please do keep your precepts.
Be energetic, resolute,
and always staunchly vigorous.

17.1.s:
Pamādaṁ bhayato disvā,
Appamādañca khemato;
Bhāvethaṭṭhaṅgikaṁ maggaṁ,
Phusantā amataṁ padan”ti.
17.1.e:
Seeing negligence as fearful,
and diligence as a sanctuary,
develop the eightfold path,
realizing the state free of death.”

17.2.s:
“Yathācārī yathāsato satīmā,
Yatasaṅkappajjhāyi appamatto;
Ajjhattarato samāhitatto,
Eko santusito tamāhu bhikkhuṁ.
17.2.e:
“One who’s mindful <j>as per their conduct and mindfulness,
diligent <j>as per their intentions and meditation,
happy inside, serene, solitary, contented:
that is what they call a mendicant.

17.2.s:
Allaṁ sukkhaṁ vā bhuñjanto,
Na bāḷhaṁ suhito siyā;
Ūnūdaro mitāhāro,
Sato bhikkhu paribbaje.
17.2.e:
When eating fresh or dried food,
one shouldn’t be overly replete.
A mendicant should wander mindfully,
with empty stomach, taking limited food.

17.2.s:
Cattāro pañca ālope,
abhutvā udakaṁ pive;
Alaṁ phāsuvihārāya,
pahitattassa bhikkhuno.
17.2.e:
Four or five mouthfuls before you’re full,
drink some water;
this is enough for a resolute mendicant
to live in comfort.

17.2.s:
Kappiyaṁ tañce chādeti,
cīvaraṁ idamatthikaṁ;
Alaṁ phāsuvihārāya,
pahitattassa bhikkhuno.
17.2.e:
If they cover themselves with a robe
that’s allowable and fit for purpose;
this is enough for a resolute mendicant
to live in comfort.

17.2.s:
Pallaṅkena nisinnassa,
jaṇṇuke nābhivassati;
Alaṁ phāsuvihārāya,
pahitattassa bhikkhuno.
17.2.e:
When sitting cross-legged,
the rain doesn’t fall on the knees;
this is enough for a resolute mendicant
to live in comfort.”

17.2.s:
Yo sukhaṁ dukkhato adda,
dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;
Ubhayantarena nāhosi,
kena lokasmi kiṁ siyā.
17.2.e:
“When you’ve seen happiness as suffering,
and suffering as a dart,
and that there’s nothing between the two—
what keeps you in the world? <j>What would you become?

17.2.s:
Mā me kadāci pāpiccho,
kusīto hīnavīriyo;
Appassuto anādaro,
kena lokasmi kiṁ siyā.
17.2.e:
Thinking, ‘May I have nothing to do <j>with those of bad wishes,
lazy, lacking energy,
unlearned, lacking regard for others’—
what keeps you in the world? <j>What would you become?”

17.2.s:
Bahussuto ca medhāvī,
sīlesu susamāhito;
Cetosamathamanuyutto,
api muddhani tiṭṭhatu.
17.2.e:
“An intelligent, learned person,
steady in ethics,
devoted to serenity of heart—
let them stand at the head.”

17.2.s:
Yo papañcamanuyutto,
papañcābhirato mago;
Virādhayī so nibbānaṁ,
yogakkhemaṁ anuttaraṁ.
17.2.e:
“A beast who likes to proliferate,
enjoying proliferation,
fails to win extinguishment,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

17.2.s:
Yo ca papañcaṁ hitvāna,
nippapañcapathe rato;
Ārādhayī so nibbānaṁ,
yogakkhemaṁ anuttaraṁ.
17.2.e:
But one who gives up proliferation,
enjoying the state of non-proliferation,
wins extinguishment,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.”

17.2.s:
Gāme vā yadi vāraññe,
Ninne vā yadi vā thale;
Yattha arahanto viharanti,
Taṁ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṁ.
17.2.e:
“Whether in the village or the wilderness,
in a valley or the uplands,
wherever the perfected ones live
is a delightful place.”

17.2.s:
Ramaṇīyāni araññāni,
yattha na ramatī jano;
Vītarāgā ramissanti,
na te kāmagavesino.
17.2.e:
“Delightful are the wildernesses
where no people delight.
Those free of greed will delight there,
not those who seek sensual pleasures.”

“Regard one who sees your faults
as a guide to a hidden treasure.
Stay close to one so intelligent and astute
who curbs you when you need it.
Sticking close to such an impartial person,
things get better, not worse.”

17.2.s:
Ovadeyyānusāseyya,
asabbhā ca nivāraye;
Satañhi so piyo hoti,
asataṁ hoti appiyo.

Aññassa bhagavā buddho,
dhammaṁ desesi cakkhumā;
Dhamme desiyamānamhi,
sotamodhesimatthiko.
17.2.e:
“The Blessed One, the Buddha, the seer
was teaching Dhamma to another.
As he taught the Dhamma,
I lent an ear to get the meaning.

17.2.s:
Taṁ me amoghaṁ savanaṁ,
vimuttomhi anāsavo.
17.2.e:
My listening wasn’t wasted:
I’m freed, without defilements.”

17.2.s:
“Rukkhamūlaṁva nissāya,
muṇḍo saṅghāṭipāruto;
Paññāya uttamo thero,
upatissova jhāyati.
17.2.e:
“His only shelter is the foot of a tree;
shaven, wrapped in his outer robe,
the senior monk foremost in wisdom,
Upatissa himself practices absorption.

17.2.s:
Avitakkaṁ samāpanno,
sammāsambuddhasāvako;
Ariyena tuṇhībhāvena,
upeto hoti tāvade.
17.2.e:
When in a meditation free of placing the mind,
a disciple of the Buddha
is at that moment blessed
with noble silence.

17.2.s:
Yathāpi pabbato selo,
acalo suppatiṭṭhito;
Evaṁ mohakkhayā bhikkhu,
pabbatova na vedhati”.
17.2.e:
As a rocky mountain
is unwavering and well grounded,
so when delusion ends,
a monk, like a mountain, doesn’t tremble.”

17.2.s:
“Anaṅgaṇassa posassa,
niccaṁ sucigavesino;
Vālaggamattaṁ pāpassa,
abbhamattaṁva khāyati.
17.2.e:
“To the man who has not a blemish,
who is always seeking purity,
even a hair-tip of evil
seems as big as a stormcloud.”

17.2.s:
Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṁ,
nābhinandāmi jīvitaṁ;
Nikkhipissaṁ imaṁ kāyaṁ,
sampajāno patissato.

Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṁ,
nābhinandāmi jīvitaṁ;
Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi,
nibbisaṁ bhatako yathā”.

“Ubhayena midaṁ maraṇameva,
Nāmaraṇaṁ pacchā vā pure vā;
Paṭipajjatha mā vinassatha,
Khaṇo vo mā upaccagā.
17.2.e:
“Both what came before and what follows after
are nothing but death, not freedom from death.
Practice, don’t perish—
don’t let the moment pass you by.

Just like a frontier city,
is guarded inside and out,
so you should ward yourselves—
don’t let the moment pass you by.
For if you miss your moment
you’ll grieve when sent to hell.”

17.2.s:
“Upasanto uparato,
mantabhāṇī anuddhato;
Dhunāti pāpake dhamme,
dumapattaṁva māluto.
17.2.e:
“Calm and still,
thoughtful in counsel, not restless—
he shakes off bad qualities
as the gale shakes leaves off a tree.

17.2.s:
Upasanto uparato,
mantabhāṇī anuddhato;
Appāsi pāpake dhamme,
dumapattaṁva māluto.
17.2.e:
Calm and still,
thoughtful in counsel, not restless—
he plucks off bad qualities
as the gale shakes leaves off a tree.

17.2.s:
Upasanto anāyāso,
vippasanno anāvilo;
Kalyāṇasīlo medhāvī,
dukkhassantakaro siyā”.
17.2.e:
Calm and free of despair,
clear and unclouded,
of good morals, intelligent:
one would make an end of suffering.”

17.2.s:
“Na vissase ekatiyesu evaṁ,
Agārisu pabbajitesu cāpi;
Sādhūpi hutvā na asādhu honti,
Asādhu hutvā puna sādhu honti.
17.2.e:
“Some householders, and even some renunciants,
are not to be trusted.
Some who were good later become bad;
while some who were bad become good.”

17.2.s:
Kāmacchando ca byāpādo,
thinamiddhañca bhikkhuno;
Uddhaccaṁ vicikicchā ca,
pañcete cittakelisā.
17.2.e:
“Sensual desire, ill will,
dullness and drowsiness,
restlessness, and doubt:
these are the five mental stains for a monk.”

17.2.s:
Yassa sakkariyamānassa,
asakkārena cūbhayaṁ;
Samādhi na vikampati,
appamādavihārino.
17.2.e:
“Whether they’re honored
or not honored, or both,
their immersion doesn’t waver
as they abide in the immeasurables.

17.2.s:
Taṁ jhāyinaṁ sātatikaṁ,
sukhumadiṭṭhivipassakaṁ;
Upādānakkhayārāmaṁ,
āhu sappuriso iti.
17.2.e:
They persistently practice absorption
with subtle view and discernment.
Rejoicing in the ending of grasping,
they’re said to be a true person.”

17.2.s:
Mahāsamuddo pathavī,
pabbato anilopi ca;
Upamāya na yujjanti,
satthu varavimuttiyā.
17.2.e:
“The oceans and the earth,
the mountains and the wind—
no simile can do justice
to the Teacher’s magnificent liberation.”

17.2.s:
Cakkānuvattako thero,
mahāñāṇī samāhito;
Pathavāpaggisamāno,
na rajjati na dussati.
17.2.e:
“The senior monk who keeps the wheel rolling,
he is very wise and serene.
Like earth, like water, like fire,
he is neither attracted nor repelled.

17.2.s:
Paññāpāramitaṁ patto,
mahābuddhi mahāmati;
Ajaḷo jaḷasamāno,
sadā carati nibbuto.
17.2.e:
He has attained the perfection of wisdom,
so intelligent and thoughtful.
He is bright, but seems to be dull;
he always wanders, quenched.”

17.2.s:
Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā,
… pe
…
bhavanetti samūhatā.
17.2.e:
“I’ve served the Teacher
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
The heavy burden is laid down,
the leash to existence is eradicated.

17.2.s:
Sampādethappamādena,
esā me anusāsanī;
Handāhaṁ parinibbissaṁ,
vippamuttomhi sabbadhī”ti.
17.2.e:
Persist with diligence:
this is my instruction.
Come, I’ll be fully quenched—
I am everywhere free.”

17.3.s:
“Pisuṇena ca kodhanena ca,
Maccharinā ca vibhūtanandinā;
Sakhitaṁ na kareyya paṇḍito,
Pāpo kāpurisena saṅgamo.
17.3.e:
“The astute would not make friends
with the slanderous or the hateful,
with a miser or a gloater,
for it’s bad to consort with reprobates.

17.3.s:
Saddhena ca pesalena ca,
Paññavatā bahussutena ca;
Sakhitaṁ kareyya paṇḍito,
Bhaddo sappurisena saṅgamo.
17.3.e:
The astute would make friends
with the faithful and the pleasant,
the wise and the learned,
for it’s a blessing to consort with true persons.”

17.3.s:
Passa cittakataṁ bimbaṁ,
… pe
…
yassa natthi dhuvaṁ ṭhiti.
17.3.e:
“See this fancy puppet,
a body built of sores,
diseased, obsessed over,
in which nothing lasts at all.

17.3.s:
Passa cittakataṁ bimbaṁ,
… pe
…
vatthehi sobhati.
17.3.e:
See this fancy puppet,
with its gems and earrings;
it is bones swathed in skin,
made pretty by its clothes.

17.3.s:
Alattakakatā,
… pe
…
no ca pāragavesino.
17.3.e:
Rouged feet
and powdered face
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.

17.3.s:
Aṭṭhapadakatā,
… pe
…
no ca pāragavesino.
17.3.e:
Hair in eight braids
and eyeshadow
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.

17.3.s:
Añjanīva navā,
… pe
…
no ca pāragavesino.
17.3.e:
A rotting body all adorned
like a freshly painted makeup box
may be enough to beguile a fool,
but not a seeker of the far shore.”

17.3.s:
Bahussuto cittakathī,
buddhassa paricārako;
Pannabhāro visaññutto,
seyyaṁ kappeti gotamo.
17.3.e:
“Gotama is learned, a brilliant speaker,
the attendant to the Buddha.
With burden put down, detached,
Gotama made his bed.

17.3.s:
Khīṇāsavo visaññutto,
saṅgātīto sunibbuto;
Dhāreti antimaṁ dehaṁ,
jātimaraṇapāragū.
17.3.e:
Defilements ended, detached,
he has got over clinging and become quenched.
He bears his final body,
having gone beyond birth and death.”

17.3.s:
Yasmiṁ patiṭṭhitā dhammā,
buddhassādiccabandhuno;
Nibbānagamane magge,
soyaṁ tiṭṭhati gotamo.
17.3.e:
“Gotama stands firm
on the path that leads to quenching,
where the teachings of the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun, are grounded.”

17.3.s:
Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṁ,
dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;
Caturāsītisahassāni,
ye me dhammā pavattino.
17.3.e:
“82,000 from the Buddha,
and 2,000 more from the monks:
84,000 teachings I’ve learned,
and these are what I promulgate.”

17.3.s:
Appassutāyaṁ puriso,
balibaddova jīrati;
Maṁsāni tassa vaḍḍhanti,
paññā tassa na vaḍḍhati.
17.3.e:
“A person of little learning
ages like an ox—
their flesh grows,
but not their wisdom.

17.3.s:
Bahussuto appassutaṁ,
yo sutenātimaññati;
Andho padīpadhārova,
tatheva paṭibhāti maṁ.
17.3.e:
A learned person who, on account of their learning,
looks down on someone of little learning,
strikes me as like
a blind man holding a lamp.

17.3.s:
Bahussutaṁ upāseyya,
sutañca na vināsaye;
Taṁ mūlaṁ brahmacariyassa,
tasmā dhammadharo siyā.
17.3.e:
You should stay close to a learned person—
don’t lose what you’ve learned.
It is the root of the spiritual life,
which is why you should memorize the teaching.

17.3.s:
Pubbāparaññū atthaññū,
niruttipadakovido;
Suggahītañca gaṇhāti,
atthañcopaparikkhati.
17.3.e:
Knowing the sequence and meaning of the teaching,
expert in the definition of terms,
they make sure it is well memorized,
and then examine the meaning.

17.3.s:
Khantyā chandikato hoti,
ussahitvā tuleti taṁ;
Samaye so padahati,
ajjhattaṁ susamāhito.
17.3.e:
Accepting the teachings, they become enthusiastic;
making an attempt, they weigh up the teaching.
When it’s time, they strive
serene inside themselves.

17.3.s:
Bahussutaṁ dhammadharaṁ,
sappaññaṁ buddhasāvakaṁ;
Dhammaviññāṇamākaṅkhaṁ,
taṁ bhajetha tathāvidhaṁ.
17.3.e:
If you want to understand the teaching,
you should befriend that sort,
who are learned and have memorized the teachings,
wise disciples of the Buddha.

17.3.s:
Bahussuto dhammadharo,
kosārakkho mahesino;
Cakkhu sabbassa lokassa,
pūjanīyo bahussuto.
17.3.e:
One who is learned <j>and has memorized the teaching,
